newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia vows to pay army debt, press on with reform.
newsitem.headline: Russia vows to pay army debt, press on with reform.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin vowed on Monday to press ahead with military reform and said he had been instructed by President Boris Yeltsin to repay all debts to the armed forces in July and August.

Speaking in the Kremlin to graduates of military academies, Chernomyrdin said he had a telephone conversation with Yeltsin earlier on Monday. He did not say what the size of the debt was, nor where the money was coming from.
Military officials say the debt, including wages to officers and funds for army maintenance, amounts to trillions, if not tens of trillions, of roubles (several billion dollars).

An influential general and senior pro-government legislator, Lev Rokhlin, last week said the government's plans to scale down the military would finally ruin the armed forces, and appealed to officers to resist.
"Without any doubt my appeal has also influenced today's announcement," he told Ekho Moskvy radio on Monday. But he said the army's budget allocation was still too small to cover its real needs.

Many political commentators have suggested Rokhlin's appeal, the first of its kind made by a respected general, was an early warning from Russia's powerful top brass, who are worried by plans to make the army a professional rather than conscript force.
The appeal was supported by Russian communists and nationalists. Rokhlin denies any political motivation, insisting the situation is critical and could lead to mutiny.
The leadership of Chernomyrdin's party Our Home is Russia, to which Rokhlin belongs, condemned his statement as a "huge political mistake" at its meeting on Monday.

"He (Rokhlin) now has to take back his statement or make all necessary conclusions," Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as telling the meeting in a clear call for the general to step down as a party member and its parliamentary deputy.

But the party leaders stopped short of expelling the general outright saying they would have to wait until all members of its faction in the State Duma lower house meet. The chamber is now on two-month summer recess.
Interfax quoted Rokhlin as telling journalists after the meeting that he had no regrets about his statement and had no plans to leave the party on his own initiative.
Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev and other ministers have already criticised it, labelling it "a call to revolution". Rokhlin said he was ready to quit the bloc if he was urged to.

However, the head of the bloc's parliamentary faction, Sergei Belyayev, said he did not expect Rokhlin to be expelled from its ranks or from his top parliament job. He said the group was likely to condemn the appeal while agreeing the situation in the army had to be improved.
Chernomyrdin also reiterated on Monday that the state of the economy made reform of the armed forces urgent.

"Delays are inadmissible. Every day costs us dear," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying. "The military reform is aimed at making the armed forces compact and mobile, but efficient and equipped with the most modern armaments and technical means."

Yeltsin, outraged by the dramatic decline of the huge but largely ineffective military machine, last year ordered Russia's 1.8-million-strong conscript army to transform itself into a smaller, battle-ready, professional force by the year 2000.
He also sacked defence minister Igor Rodionov for failing to start the long-delayed reform and whining about the poor state of the army. He put Sergeyev in charge last month.
